1:
The letter opens without a title, and the commentators treat the omission as evidence, not accident. Gill reports the reasons as variously conjectured — that Paul was well enough known there to need no epithet, that a pompous title might have made young converts stumble, or that no false apostles were present to force the claim. Henry takes the last of these: the apostleship was neither doubted at Thessalonica nor opposed there, so nothing required asserting. Ellicott agrees a church so familiar needed no reminder, noting the same omission in Philippians and Philemon; but he refuses two explanations built on it — an early date, or courtesy to his companions — as disproved by 1 Thessalonians 2:6. Calvin turns the silence into a compliment: where Paul elsewhere designates himself an Apostle it is to claim a contested authority, so the bare name is evidence that these hearers acknowledged him voluntarily and received his doctrine with reverence.

On the names joined to his, Chrysostom asks why Timothy appears here and not in the letter to Ephesus, and answers that Paul was about to send him, so writing was superfluous. Henry reads the joining as humility and as an honour deliberately put upon ministers of inferior rank; Ellicott gives Silas precedence as the man of higher standing. Robertson supplies the biography — Silvanus a Jew and Roman citizen, Timothy the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father — and insists neither is in any sense the author, the nominative absolute being customary letter form. Barnes gives the setting instead: Thessalonica the seaport of Macedonia at the head of the Thermaic gulf. Clarke adds that the city was named by Philip of Macedon for his victory over the Thessalians or from Cassander’s wife, and was taken from the Venetians by the Turks in 1431. Tertullian’s block runs past the salutation into the body of the letter, arguing against an apostle of a rival god: the Jews who slew their prophets and then the Lord sinned against one Lord.

The thanksgiving draws a common insistence. Gill takes it as covering every member — Jew or Gentile, rich or poor, officer or private Christian — and presses that Paul ascribes nothing to their free will, dispositions, or diligence, and nothing to himself or his companions, who were only ministers. Calvin makes the same point a pastoral instrument: praise of their virtues is a spur to perseverance rather than congratulation, since recognising the gifts as God’s humbles a pious mind where confidence in supposed virtues makes it careless. Ellicott reads “to God” the same way, that none of the success is due to preachers or converts, and glosses “always” not as without ceasing but as on every occasion that recalls them. Henry makes thanksgiving itself the duty, to be performed constantly, and offered not only for favours we receive but for benefits given to others. Barnes draws two inferences from the mention of prayer: that Paul prayed constantly, and extemporaneously, since forms could not have been adapted to churches still being organised. Robertson notes that the plural implies all three missionaries prayed together.

On the triad, Ellicott notes that in this first of his writings Paul has already fixed the three abiding principles and reads each genitive as an emphatic adjective — faithful activity, loving labour, hopeful endurance — governed throughout by “in our Lord.” Clarke works the same distinction as a gradation: faith not speculative but operative, love labouring because it can do more, hope not impatient to escape trial but willing to endure where God is most honoured by the endurance. Wesley compresses it to a line — faith works, love labours, hope patiently suffers all things — adding that those who do not thus labour do not love. Robertson notes the article with both nouns; Gill takes the remembering as the reason for the mention, not a separate act.
4:
Verse 4 divides the readers. Gill takes the election as the eternal choice of persons to everlasting life, made by the Father in Christ before the world began, and rules out three lesser senses — election to an office, since the letter is to the whole church; election to the Gospel as an outward means, common to them with others; and effectual calling, which the next verse names as this election’s fruit. Clarke denies exactly that: what they knew was that God had chosen the Gentiles to the privileges the Jews had rejected, and no unconditional, eternal and personal election to everlasting glory is meant. Ellicott stands nearer Clarke, taking election in Paul and Peter as primarily a gracious admission into religious privileges in this life, implying nothing as to a person’s final condition; Wesley adds only that it is known through faith, by these plain proofs. Two further questions attach. Barnes reports the marginal pointing, “beloved of God, your election,” and thinks the sense not materially varied, where Ellicott holds the Greek idiom cannot allow the Authorised rendering at all. On whose knowing is meant, Barnes refers it to Paul, Silas and Timothy; Calvin prefers Chrysostom’s reading, which does the same, to the one Erasmus gave the Thessalonians.

The evidence follows. Barnes sets out the structure: election is proved first by the manner in which the gospel was received, then by the spirit they showed in sending it abroad. Gill explains “our gospel” as neither authored by the preachers nor about them, but committed to their trust, over against what the false teachers preached. Clarke and Wesley take the power as felt: Clarke as miraculous manifestation to eye and heart, with a change of heart and life pressed in place of any rite; Wesley as a piercing of the heart with the sense of sin, the Holy Ghost testifying outwardly by miracles and by descent through laying on of hands, and full assurance coming as the Spirit sheds the love of God abroad. Ellicott decides against them on whose power is meant: the preachers’ own, not the people’s, as “as ye know” proves. Robertson leaves the connecting particle undecided between “because,” “how that,” and a merely explanatory use. Calvin reads the whole as design: God honoured Paul’s ministry in order to manifest their adoption to them.

On imitation the voices converge, then qualify. Henry finds the apostles’ preaching and living all of a piece, so that the Thessalonians, observing what manner of men they were, imitated them conscientiously. Barnes denies this made the preachers heads of a sect — only their manner of living was copied — and infers that the Saviour’s life must have been a prominent topic in the preaching and a means of their conversion. Robertson calls it a daring thing to expect imitation of a preacher, and finds the safeguard in the added “and of the Lord.” Gill limits the following the same way, noting the Alexandrian copy reads “of God” and others “of Christ.” Ellicott itemises three points imitated: meek reception, at whatever cost, with rejoicing throughout. Clarke says the consolations more than counterbalanced the persecutions; Wesley reduces it to a clause, though in much affliction, yet with much joy. Calvin makes the correspondence itself the proof, a harmony between the preaching and the faith.

Verse 7 turns the imitators into a pattern. Barnes traces the word to a mark left by a blow, then a die, then a model; Clarke gives types and patterns for creed and conduct; Gill makes them patterns of good works and of suffering. Robertson notes the manuscripts divide between singular and plural, the singular viewing the church as a whole; Ellicott prefers the singular for that reason, and adds that Macedonia and Achaia comprised all Roman Greece. Calvin thinks it a great thing to have so outstripped those who entered the course first.
8:
Verse 8 draws one figure from nearly everyone, with different mechanics behind it. Gill takes “sounded out” as an allusion to the blowing of a trumpet, and defines the word of the Lord three ways — from him as author, of him as subject, by him as dispenser — so that it is received not as the word of man. Barnes presses the trumpet further, an echo and re-echo among the hills and vales of Greece, and adds that the diffusion was at first involuntary, a necessary result of conversion rather than a deliberate purpose. Robertson notes the verb occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and reaches for a modern figure, the church as a sounding board or transmitting station, while conceding a pardonable touch of hyperbole. Calvin calls it an elegant metaphor and takes it plainly: their faith was so lively that it roused other nations, and the matter no longer required publishing by him. Clarke and Wesley supply the physical means — Thessalonica a city of great commerce, well situated for traffic, whose merchants carried the report abroad; Clarke adds that the converts had walked so conscientiously that friends could speak of them without a blush and adversaries could say nothing to their disgrace. Ellicott corrects the tense, has rung out rather than rang, notes the clauses are not quite balanced, and glosses “your faith” as the report of their faith, not their creed. Chrysostom alone begins elsewhere, from ointment that will not keep its fragrance shut up but scents the air: illustrious men likewise benefit many by their good report.

On who is speaking in verse 9 the readings differ. Gill takes it of those to whom the reports were brought; Ellicott of the inhabitants of the countries named, so that wherever the preachers go they find their own story told them; Robertson of the men of Macedonia, stressing both that they do it voluntarily and that the present tense means they keep on reporting. Barnes turns the testimony back on the preachers: what is said of the Thessalonians is evidence of how the gospel was preached among them, and shows they were not actuated by selfish or sinister motives. Clarke reads the turning from idols as decisive for the make-up of the church — it could be said neither of Jews nor of the devout persons, so the majority must have been heathen Greeks — and unfolds the two adjectives, living against stocks and stones and the representations of dead men, true against a system false in its objects, pretensions, promises and prospects. Calvin sees the sentence state in order what man’s condition is before the gospel enlightens him, to what end God instructs us, and what the gospel’s fruit is.

The last clause carries the substantial disagreement. Robertson observes that the infinitive is linear, to keep on waiting, and that the hope of the second coming was real and powerful with Paul though open to abuse then as now. Barnes finds the return a prominent subject of the preaching at Thessalonica but declines to infer it was pressed there more than elsewhere. Ellicott makes the two infinitives describe not the converts’ intention in turning but the condition into which turning brought them, and shifts both tenses: better delivereth, and better a wrath already coming, from which Christ is day by day saving us. Wesley divides it the same way — redeemed once, delivered continually, delivered at last from the eternal vengeance. Clarke alone gives the wrath a historical reference beside the penal one, the destruction about to come on the unbelieving and impenitent Jews. Gill and Calvin both anchor the waiting in resurrection: Gill in the eternal Sonship of one who ascended and will return to judge the world, Calvin in Christ’s own rising, since our minds give way unless we look to him, and he rose that his members might share his glory.
